where: Section 1, the sentence that sets I*
problem: "A DC-link or MPPT loop compares available DC power with delivered AC power and sets I*" blends two different functions. MPPT hunts the PV operating point; it does not compare DC power with AC power. The block that actually produces the active current reference is the DC-link voltage controller, which reacts to the power imbalance.
fix: The DC-link voltage controller sets I*: if the DC-link voltage sags, the inverter must deliver more AC power, so I* rises. MPPT, where present, moves the DC operating point (or gives the DC power reference) so the DC link sits at its set value.

problem: The text says the amplitude "follows the power demand and the reactive limit" without stating the catch: at a fixed I*, changing φ* also changes real power, because P = V_rms I_rms cos φ. A student can conclude that φ* shifts reactive power alone.
fix: Add: holding I* fixed while moving φ* reduces real power (cos φ falls), so I* must be recomputed for the wanted P* and Q*: I_rms = √(P*² + Q*²)/V_rms, with Q* = V_rms I_rms sin φ*.

problem: Two different faults (commanding a voltage amplitude, and omitting the PLL) are joined to one consequence (wrong phase and reactive power). Commanding voltage amplitude gives an uncontrolled current set by the impedance difference, not necessarily a wrong phase.
fix: Split the bullet. Commanding a voltage amplitude on a grid-tied inverter leaves the current set by the small impedance difference, i.e. uncontrolled. Omitting the PLL loses θ, so the current reference lands at the wrong phase and the inverter exchanges unwanted reactive power.

problem: "A current loop often runs at 1–2 kHz" is ambiguous: 1–2 kHz is the achievable closed-loop bandwidth, while the switching and sampling frequencies are much higher. A student may read it as the PWM switching frequency.
fix: A current loop has a bandwidth of about 1–2 kHz; the PWM switching and sampling run higher, typically several kHz to tens of kHz.
